lessons.title: Natural breeding: paddock and in-hand
lessons.html:
Choosing a breeding method

Each breeding method has advantages, risks and costs. The right choice depends on the breed society rules, the value of the horses, the facilities and skills available, and disease risks. For example, the Thoroughbred studbook only accepts foals from natural live cover; artificial insemination and embryo transfer are not allowed. Many sport horse and Arabian societies do allow them. Always check the breed society rules before breeding.

Paddock or free breeding

The stallion runs with a group of mares in a camp and covers them as they come into season, as in the wild.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Natural, low stress for maresHigh risk of kicks and injury to the stallion
Little labour and few facilitiesExact service dates are unknown, so foaling dates are uncertain
Good conception rates when mares are well fedDisease can spread between all animals
Suits extensive farms, e.g. Boerperd or Basotho pony herdsLimits the number of mares per stallion

To assess it, check that the mares are known to the stallion, that the camp is safe with no wire hazards, that mares have been checked by a vet, and that the herd is observed daily.

In-hand breeding

The mare and stallion are each held by a trained handler. The mare is teased first to confirm she is in season, often checked by the vet with rectal palpation or ultrasound to time ovulation.

  • Advantages: exact service dates, control of the number of covers, better safety for the stallion, and hygiene can be applied.
  • Disadvantages: needs skilled staff, a safe breeding area with non-slip footing, and more time.
  • Safety: the mare may wear hind boots or a twitch; handlers wear helmets and stand to the side, never behind the horses.

Hygiene in both methods includes washing the stallion's penis with clean warm water only and the mare's vulva area before service, and screening for venereal diseases as advised by the vet.

lessons.title: Assisted reproduction: AI and embryo transfer
lessons.html:
Artificial insemination (AI)

Semen is collected from the stallion using an artificial vagina and a dummy mount or a mare in season. It is checked under a microscope, diluted with an extender and used fresh, chilled or frozen.

  • Fresh semen is used on the same farm within hours.
  • Chilled semen is cooled and couriered, and normally used within about a day or two.
  • Frozen semen is stored in liquid nitrogen and can be imported from overseas, subject to veterinary import permits.
AdvantagesDisadvantages
No risk of injury from coveringNeeds a vet and laboratory equipment
One collection can breed several maresExact timing to ovulation is needed, especially with frozen semen
Access to top stallions far awayNot allowed by some breed societies
Reduces spread of venereal diseaseHigher cost per cycle

Embryo transfer (ET)

The donor mare is inseminated. About a week after ovulation, the vet flushes the embryo from her uterus and places it into a recipient mare whose cycle has been synchronised with the donor's. The recipient carries the foal and raises it.

  • When it is used: valuable competition mares that must keep competing, older mares that cannot carry a foal, or to get several foals in one season from one top mare.
  • Requirements: a skilled vet, a group of healthy recipient mares of suitable size, hormone synchronisation and good records.
  • Disadvantages: high cost, lower success per attempt than natural breeding, and breed society restrictions.

Assessing which method to use

  1. Check breed society rules.
  2. Consider the value and health of mare and stallion.
  3. Assess facilities, staff skill and access to a vet.
  4. Compare costs in ZAR per pregnancy.
  5. Consider disease control and record keeping.

Key points

  • Breed society rules come first; Thoroughbreds need natural live cover.
  • Paddock breeding is cheap and natural but risky and gives uncertain dates.
  • In-hand breeding gives control and exact dates but needs skilled handlers.
  • AI uses fresh, chilled or frozen semen and reduces injury and disease risk.
  • Embryo transfer lets a valuable mare produce foals carried by recipient mares.
